justification: This session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (shared across concurrently running critics/agents) before I could search fresh, and direct WebFetch attempts at the usual vendor/blog results for "tcp vs udp" (Cloudflare, GeeksforGeeks, Fortinet, Imperva, Kinsta, Baeldung, Comparitech, AWS) all returned 403/404 to the fetcher. I compared instead against the two pages I could actually read that anchor the top results for TCP and UDP individually and that a technical reader would trust: Wikipedia's Transmission Control Protocol and User Datagram Protocol articles, both confirmed (via fetch) to give detailed, RFC-grounded, bit-level coverage including, for TCP, a dedicated congestion-control section (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery) -- neither has runnable code or real measurements. Verification performed: ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/networking/tcp-vs-udp.md` myself (PASS, 17 blocks/8 executed). Independently re-ran the three 'surprising' programs outside the harness on this machine: the TCP flow-control stall reproduced at exactly write 560 / 2,289,664 bytes (matches the article's 'around 560 writes, roughly 2.3 MB' -- 2,289,664 B is 2.29 MB in decimal SI units); the UDP send-storm with the explicit ReceiveBufferSize removed reproduced exactly 'receiver saw 64 of 200', matching the exercise solution verbatim; the connected-UdpClient-to-nobody-listening program reproduced 'receive failed: ConnectionReset' exactly. All three surprising claims hold. I opened and checked every quoted sentence against its primary source: RFC 9293 section 2.2 ('TCP provides a reliable, in-order, byte-stream service to applications'), section 3.7 (the segment/buffer-boundary sentence), section 3.5 (three-way handshake), section 3.1 (Window field), section 3.8.1 ('the retransmission timeout (RTO) must be dynamically determined', RFC 6298), section 3.6 (FIN/TIME-WAIT, 2xMSL); RFC 768 (the 'minimum of protocol mechanism' quote and the 8-byte, four-field header); RFC 8085 section 1 (congestion-collapse/fairness quote), 3.1.2 (TFRC/window-based recommendation), 3.1.3 (one datagram per RTT); RFC 9000 section 1 ('QUIC packets are carried in UDP datagrams ... to better facilitate deployment', TLS integration) and section 2 (streams ordered internally, not ordered relative to each other); RFC 792 (Destination Unreachable is a 'may', not a 'must'); RFC 1035 section 4.2.1 (512-byte UDP limit, truncation/TC bit). Every one is verbatim-accurate and attached to the sentence it actually supports; no fabricated or misattributed citation found, and all eight front-matter sources are cited inline. All eight programs are complete, idiomatic, modern C# and match their shown output. What keeps this below the 8.5 (MDN/Real-Python-with-nits) anchor is a real depth gap, not an error: the content plan's own outline for this slug calls for 'flow/congestion control', and the article thoroughly builds and demonstrates flow control (the receive window, with a working stall demo) but never explains TCP's own congestion control (slow start, AIMD, the congestion window) as a distinct mechanism -- the phrase appears exactly once, unexplained and uncited, in the summary table ('Flow and congestion control slow the sender down'), and the only place 'congestion control' gets real treatment in the article is RFC 8085's requirement that UDP-based applications build their own. A reader who has just read the flow-control section could easily come away thinking that receiver-driven window management is the whole story, which every serious competing reference (including both Wikipedia pages read for this review) treats as a separate, essential mechanism. That, plus two smaller nits below, is why this lands at 8.0 rather than higher.

issues.location: "What each one actually promises" table, "Pace" row ("Flow and congestion control slow the sender down"), and the absence of any other mention of TCP's own congestion control anywhere in the body (grep confirms the phrase appears only in that table cell and, separately, three times in the QUIC/RFC 8085 section about what UDP-based applications must build for themselves)
issues.problem: The article's own planned outline (CONTENT_PLAN.md section 7, row for tcp-vs-udp) calls for 'flow/congestion control' as one of the topics, and the table asserts TCP does congestion control, but the concept is never explained, demonstrated or cited anywhere -- unlike every other guarantee in that same table, which gets a full section, a runnable program and an RFC citation. Flow control (the receive window, RWND) and congestion control (the congestion window, CWND, driven by network loss/delay rather than receiver capacity) are two distinct mechanisms that TCP courses and every competing reference for this exact query (e.g. Wikipedia's TCP article, which gives congestion control its own section covering slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery) treat separately; conflating them or leaving one entirely unglossed is exactly the kind of gap a strong CS student would flag. It is also a sourcing gap: RFC 5681 (TCP congestion control), the RFC that would actually support this table cell, is not in the source list at all.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add a short paragraph or subsection after (or inside) "Flow control: the receiver sets TCP's pace" that names congestion control as the second, distinct reason a TCP sender slows down: driven by inferred network conditions (loss/delay) via the congestion window, not by what the receiver has said it can hold, with a citation to the actual congestion-control RFC (RFC 5681, or RFC 9293's own references to it) added to the source list. A full slow-start demo is not required on loopback (which essentially never signals congestion), but the article should say why loopback can't show it and cite the mechanism precisely rather than leaving it as an unglossed word in a table cell.

issues.location: "Framing a stream yourself" section, WriteFramed/ReadFramed helper functions (BitConverter.GetBytes(payload.Length) / BitConverter.ToInt32(header))
issues.problem: The length-prefix header is written and read with BitConverter's platform (little-endian on x64) byte order and no explicit note that this only works because both ends of this loopback demo run on the same machine. Every real wire protocol built this way (the article calls this scheme representative of 'what every text protocol built on TCP does one way or another') has to fix the byte order explicitly, since two peers on different architectures would disagree on what the 4 header bytes mean. A strong student implementing this for real would hit that immediately.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either switch the header read/write to an explicit byte order (e.g. System.Buffers.Binary.BinaryPrimitives.WriteInt32BigEndian/ReadInt32BigEndian, or IPAddress.HostToNetworkOrder) and say why, or add one sentence noting that this demo relies on both ends sharing endianness and that a real cross-machine protocol must pick and document a byte order for the length prefix.
